clinicalPearls: Inherited bone marrow failure syndrome of defective DNA interstrand crosslink repair, caused by biallelic (or X-linked/heterozygous in rare subtypes) variants in one of many FANC genes constituting the Fanconi anaemia/BRCA pathway.

Classic congenital features include short stature, radial ray and thumb anomalies, abnormal skin pigmentation (cafe-au-lait macules), microcephaly and renal or urogenital malformations, though a substantial minority have few or no anomalies.
Progressive bone marrow failure typically emerges in the first decade, often beginning with thrombocytopenia or macrocytosis and evolving to pancytopenia.
There is a markedly increased risk of myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukaemia, and of solid tumours, especially head-and-neck and anogenital squamous cell carcinoma.
The diagnostic hallmark is increased chromosomal breakage in lymphocytes exposed to DNA crosslinking agents such as diepoxybutane or mitomycin C.
Patients are exquisitely sensitive to conventional chemotherapy and radiotherapy, mandating substantial dose modification and specialist input.

Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can correct the haematological disease but does not abolish, and may increase, the risk of subsequent solid tumours, so lifelong cancer surveillance is essential.
reference.pathophysiology: Fanconi anaemia is a genetically heterogeneous disorder of genome maintenance caused by biallelic variants (with rare X-linked and dominant-acting exceptions) in genes encoding components of the Fanconi anaemia/BRCA DNA-repair pathway. This pathway coordinates the recognition and repair of DNA interstrand crosslinks that arise during replication: a core multiprotein complex monoubiquitinates the FANCD2-FANCI heterodimer, which is recruited to sites of crosslink-stalled replication forks and orchestrates downstream nucleolytic incision, translesion synthesis and homologous recombination involving downstream partners including BRCA2. Loss of pathway function leads to accumulation of unrepaired crosslinks, chromosomal breakage and radial-figure formation, replication stress, cell-cycle arrest and excessive apoptosis of haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, producing progressive marrow failure. The same genomic instability, compounded by aberrant clonal selection, drives the strong predisposition to myelodysplasia, acute myeloid leukaemia and squamous carcinomas, and explains the profound cellular hypersensitivity to crosslinking chemotherapy and ionising radiation.
additionalDifferentials: Other inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, Diamond-Blackfan anaemia)
Thrombocytopenia-absent-radius syndrome and other radial-ray disorders
Nijmegen breakage syndrome and other chromosomal instability disorders
additionalInvestigations: Chromosome breakage/fragility test with diepoxybutane or mitomycin C
Full blood count and blood film (macrocytosis, cytopenias)
Bone marrow aspirate, trephine and cytogenetics for hypocellularity and clonal change
Molecular genetic testing across the panel of FANC/DNA-repair genes
Somatic mosaicism assessment when blood testing is equivocal (e.g. fibroblast studies)
Renal and skeletal imaging for congenital anomalies
HLA typing and organ-specific cancer surveillance including head-and-neck and gynaecological examination
redFlags: New or worsening cytopenias suggesting evolving marrow failure
Cytogenetic clonal abnormality or dysplasia indicating transformation to MDS/AML
Suspicious mucosal or skin lesion suggesting squamous cell carcinoma
Unexpectedly severe toxicity after chemotherapy or radiotherapy
Severe bleeding or infection from profound pancytopenia
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is determined chiefly by the pace of marrow failure and the high lifetime risk of leukaemia and solid tumours; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can cure the marrow disease but survivors require lifelong surveillance because the cancer predisposition persists. Outcomes have improved with modified transplant regimens and structured cancer screening, but the disorder remains life-limiting.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis on physical appearance alone, since many patients lack overt congenital anomalies
Administering standard-dose chemotherapy or radiotherapy and causing catastrophic toxicity
Missing the diagnosis because of somatic mosaicism giving a falsely reassuring blood breakage test
Assuming transplantation removes cancer risk and stopping solid-tumour surveillance
Attributing isolated macrocytosis or mild thrombocytopenia to benign causes and delaying breakage testing
references: Standard textbook of paediatric and adult haematology
Clinical genetics reference texts on inherited bone marrow failure and chromosomal instability syndromes
Consensus guidelines for diagnosis and management of Fanconi anaemia
management: Treat progressive marrow failure with allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, the only curative option for the haematological disease
Use androgen therapy such as oxymetholone or danazol to stimulate haematopoiesis, with transfusion support and iron chelation while transplant is deferred or awaited
Apply substantial dose reduction of chemotherapy and radiotherapy under specialist guidance owing to extreme crosslinker and radiation hypersensitivity
Institute lifelong surveillance for myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukaemia with regular blood counts and bone marrow examination with cytogenetics
Screen actively for head-and-neck and anogenital squamous cell carcinoma, advising tobacco and alcohol avoidance and offering HPV vaccination
Refer to a multidisciplinary team addressing endocrine complications such as short stature, diabetes and thyroid dysfunction alongside congenital anomalies
Provide genetic counselling with cascade family screening and consideration of an HLA-matched sibling donor
